title: Daily Sales to Seasonal Trends
text:
If you’ve ever worked retail you know the feeling. One week the store is dead and the next week everyone needs a winter coat and you’re sold out of everything good. That’s not random. Sales go up and down in a pattern that repeats every year and if you can spot it early you can plan for it instead of scrambling after it happens.
I wanted to see that pattern in an actual chart and it turns out it’s not too hard. In this tutorial I’ll show you how to take daily sales add them up by month and plot the result so the seasons jump out at you. You only need basic Python and a little bit of pandas.

title: Daily Sales to Seasonal Trends
text:
The Tools
We’re using three libraries:

pandas for organizing and grouping the data
numpy for making up our practice data
matplotlib for the chart

I recommend just pulling data from H&M fashion Dataset on Kaggle or a similar website, and this should come with retail datat already. If you want to follow along with my code the data I used is on my GitHub.

title: Daily Sales to Seasonal Trends
text:
Building the Chart

Imports

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt



Making the Data
The fake sales have three pieces: a baseline (what the store normally sells in a day), a seasonal bump (higher in winter, lower in summer), and noise (random daily ups and downs, because real life is messy). I also added a slow upward trend so it looks like the store is growing.

rng = np.random.default_rng(386)  # seed so you get the same data I did

dates = pd.date_range("2023-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D")
month = dates.month

base = 100
seasonal = 40 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (month - 12) / 12)  # peaks in December
trend = np.linspace(0, 15, len(dates))
noise = rng.normal(0, 10, len(dates))

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "date": dates,
    "sales": (base + seasonal + trend + noise).round(2),
})
df.head()

df.head() shows the first five rows: one row per day with that day’s sales. The whole table has 731 rows, which is way too many to look at one by one, so that’s our next problem.


Wrangling
Daily sales are super bouncy, so it’s hard to see any pattern. Adding them up by month fixes that:

monthly = df.groupby(df["date"].dt.to_period("M"))["sales"].sum()
monthly.head()

date
2023-01    4077.56
2023-02    3316.28
2023-03    3148.97
2023-04    2393.76
2023-05    2146.46
Freq: M, Name: sales, dtype: float64


The main thing we need to do here is group the rows by month and add up the sales in each group. Here’s what each part does:

df["date"].dt.to_period("M"): turns each date into its month, so January 5th and January 20th both become “2023-01”
df.groupby(...): puts all the rows from the same month into one group
["sales"].sum(): adds up the sales in each group

Now we have 24 numbers instead of 731.


Visualization
Now for the best part! Here’s the code, and then I’ll break it down.

monthly.plot(kind="line", marker="o")
plt.title("Monthly Sales (2023-2024)")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Total Sales")
plt.show()









monthly.plot(kind="line", marker="o"): draws the line, with a dot for each month
plt.title(), plt.xlabel(), plt.ylabel(): label the chart so people know what they’re looking at
plt.show(): displays it

You should see two big humps, one around each winter, with a dip in between. That’s the seasonality. The pattern repeats, so if it happened last December, it’s probably going to happen this December too.
You might also notice the whole line drifts up over time. That’s the trend, and it’s different from seasonality. Seasonality goes up and down every year, while a trend keeps heading in one direction.

title: Daily Sales to Seasonal Trends
text:
Why This Matters
If you know sales jump every winter, you can stock up before the rush, schedule more people, and plan your promotions around it. This is also the basic idea behind forecasting. The fancy models that predict future sales are mostly doing a fancier version of this: finding the repeating pattern and projecting it forward.

title: Daily Sales to Seasonal Trends
text:
Wrapping It Up
In this tutorial, you should have learned how to turn a pile of daily sales into a chart that shows the seasons, using groupby, .dt.to_period(), and a simple line plot. Even if it looked intimidating at first, it’s really just grouping your data and plotting it.
Now that you know how to do it, here are some things to try:

Change "M" to "Q" to group by quarter and see how the chart changes
Make the seasonal bump bigger in the fake data and see how the chart reacts
Try it on real data, like the H&M dataset linked above

Happy plotting!
